vessels.name: PAUL R TREGURTHA
vessels.fact: Queen of the Lakes — longest ship on the Great Lakes, 1,013 ft
vessels.source: interlake-steamship.com (1013.5 ft, Queen of the Lakes since 1981)
facts: Queen of the Lakes — longest ship on the Great Lakes, 1,013 ft
She originally sailed as the William J. DeLancey and was renamed Paul R. Tregurtha in 1990.
She was the last ship ever built at the American Ship Building yard in Lorain, Ohio.
She was the last of the Great Lakes' thirteen thousand-footers to enter service.
Her plush owner's quarters and onboard elevator earned her the nickname Fancy DeLancey.

vessels.name: VIKING OCTANTIS
vessels.fact: Largest cruise ship sailing the Great Lakes — 673 ft
vessels.source: seatrade-cruise.com / urbanmilwaukee.com 2025 (polar-rating claim dropped, unverified; sources vary 665-673 ft)
facts: Largest cruise ship sailing the Great Lakes — 673 ft
She is named for Sigma Octantis, the faint star that marks the South Pole.
Her sister ship, Viking Polaris, takes her name from Polaris, the North Star.
She carries two bright yellow submersibles that take guests diving beneath the surface.
She was built in Romania at a VARD shipyard owned by Italy's Fincantieri.

vessels.name: LEO A.MCARTHUR
vessels.fact: Tug that pushes a heated liquid-asphalt barge year-round
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/leo-a-mcarthur (built 2009 as Victorious, renamed 2017; mated to heated asphalt barge John J. Carrick, year-round). Length 122 ft not confirmed — zeroed.
facts: Tug that pushes a heated liquid-asphalt barge year-round
She first sailed as the Victorious before being renamed Leo A. McArthur in 2017.
She locks to her barge, the John J. Carrick, with a hinged Articouple coupling system.

vessels.name: FLORENCE SPIRIT
vessels.fact: Collided head-on in the Welland Canal in 2020 — both survived
vessels.source: TSB Canada report M20C0188 (11 July 2020 collision with Alanis). Corrected: it was an actual head-on collision, not a 'near' miss; 'went viral' unverified and removed. Length 447 ft not confirmed — zeroed.
facts: Collided head-on in the Welland Canal in 2020 — both survived
She was built in 2004 in Shimonoseki, Japan.
She first sailed as the Irish-owned Arklow Willow before coming to Canada.
She is named for Florence, the wife of McKeil Marine's founder Evans McKeil.

vessels.name: ALGOMA NIAGARA
vessels.fact: First Equinox-class self-unloader built for Algoma
vessels.source: drybulkmagazine.com / businesswire.com 2017 (first Equinox-class self-unloader; earlier Equinox ships were gearless). Length 740 ft not confirmed — zeroed.
facts: First Equinox-class self-unloader built for Algoma
She was built in Jingjiang, China, at the Yangzijiang shipyard.
She sailed roughly two months from China to Canada via the Panama Canal.
Her near-identical sister self-unloader is the Algoma Sault.
She was designed to be about 45 percent more fuel-efficient than the older ships in her fleet.

vessels.name: OLIVE L. MOORE
vessels.fact: Built 1928 — still pushing barges after 97 years
vessels.source: boatnerd.com / masoncountypress.com May 2025 (launched 16 Apr 1928 as John F. Cushing; confirmed still working with barge Menominee)
facts: Built 1928 — still pushing barges after 97 years
She was built as the John F. Cushing for a Chicago dredging company.
She was rebuilt as an articulated tug in 1991 to push the barge McKee Sons.

vessels.name: HON JAMES L OBERSTAR
vessels.fact: Built 1959, stretched 96 ft in 1972 — now 806 ft long
vessels.source: boatnerd.com / interlake-steamship.com (built 1959 as Shenango II, lengthened 96 ft at Fraser Shipyards 1972, now 806.0 ft)
facts: Built 1959, stretched 96 ft in 1972 — now 806 ft long
She first sailed as the Shenango II, built for the Shenango Furnace Company.
She honors a Minnesota congressman who long chaired the House Transportation Committee.
At his own request, her renaming was held off until her 2011 christening, after he had left Congress.
She was rebuilt into a self-unloader in 1981.

vessels.name: STERLING ENERGY
vessels.fact: A floating gas station — refuels other ships in port
vessels.source: sterlingfuels.ca / seawayreview.com / vesselfinder IMO 9277058 (bunkering tanker, built 2002, 64 m = 210 ft; corrected from 213 ft). Upgraded from medium to high.
facts: A floating gas station — refuels other ships in port
She was built in 2002 and first sailed under the Turkish flag as the Melisa-D.
At about 210 feet, she's a small oil-products tanker beside the freighters around her.

vessels.name: ALGOMA DISCOVERY
vessels.fact: Gearless bulk carrier built 1987 — no self-unloading boom
vessels.source: Wikipedia Algoma Central fleet list (1987, gearless bulk carrier, in service). Croatian-build claim could NOT be verified and was removed. Length 729 ft not confirmed — zeroed.
facts: Gearless bulk carrier built 1987 — no self-unloading boom
She was launched in Croatia as the Malinska, at Rijeka's 3 Maj shipyard.
She sailed as Norway's Daviken before Algoma purchased her in 2008.
She ranks among the largest saltwater-built ships ever to sail the Great Lakes.

vessels.name: EEMSBORG
vessels.fact: Dutch-flagged 'salty' — an ocean ship visiting the Lakes
vessels.source: vesselfinder IMO 9423748 (general cargo ship, built 2009, Netherlands flag, 137.84 m = 452 ft; corrected from 453 ft)
facts: Dutch-flagged 'salty' — an ocean ship visiting the Lakes
She was built in Delfzijl, Netherlands, at the Royal Niestern Sander shipyard.
She was christened during Delfsail, a huge Dutch maritime festival, in 2009.
In 2013 she lost power and ran aground in the St. Lawrence River.

vessels.name: EDWIN H. GOTT
vessels.fact: 1,004 ft — longest self-unloading boom on the Great Lakes
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Edwin_H._Gott
facts: 1,004 ft — longest self-unloading boom on the Great Lakes
She's named for Edwin H. Gott, a former chairman and chief executive of United States Steel.
She was built in 1979 at Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin.
In the winter of 2010 to 2011 her original Enterprise diesels were replaced with modern MaK engines.

vessels.name: FRONTENAC
vessels.fact: Helped search for the Edmund Fitzgerald in 1975
vessels.source: greatlakesships.wordpress.com/frontenac/ · cslships.com/vessel/frontenac
facts: Helped search for the Edmund Fitzgerald in 1975
She was built in 1968 by Davie Shipbuilding at Lauzon, Quebec.
She was the last traditional-styled lake freighter ever built for Canada Steamship Lines.
After about five years hauling ore, she was rebuilt as a self-unloader at Collingwood.

vessels.name: LEE A. TREGURTHA
vessels.fact: WWII Navy oiler USS Chiwawa — earned two battle stars
vessels.source: interlake-steamship.com · en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Chiwawa
facts: WWII Navy oiler USS Chiwawa — earned two battle stars
The name Chiwawa came from a river in Washington State.
Over her long career she has sailed under four different names.
In 2006 her old steam plant was replaced with a modern diesel plant.
Her current name honors Lee Tregurtha, wife of Interlake's vice chairman.

vessels.name: PERELIK
vessels.fact: Bulgarian-run saltie named for the Rhodopes' highest peak
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 9905722 · en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golyam_Perelik
facts: Bulgarian-run saltie named for the Rhodopes' highest peak
Though Bulgarian-owned by Navibulgar, she sails under the flag of Malta.

vessels.name: SEA EAGLE II
vessels.fact: 7,200 hp pusher tug coupled into a cement barge as one unit
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/sea-eagle-ii/
facts: 7,200 hp pusher tug coupled into a cement barge as one unit
She was built in 1979 in Houma, Louisiana, and first named simply Sea Eagle.
In 1981 she was sold to Canadian Marine Drilling of Calgary and renamed Canmar Sea Eagle.
St. Marys Cement bought her in 1991 and renamed her Sea Eagle II.

vessels.name: STORMONT
vessels.fact: Built 1953 — still pushing barges after 70+ years
vessels.source: mckeil.com/our-fleet/stormont/ · gltugs.wordpress.com/stormont/
facts: Built 1953 — still pushing barges after 70+ years
She was built in 1953 by the Canadian Dredge and Dock Company for Ontario's government.
She joined the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority fleet in 1964.
For decades she powered the Detroit-to-Windsor truck ferry across the river, until the service ended in 2023.

vessels.name: MACCOA
vessels.fact: Canfornav names its whole fleet after ducks — this one too
vessels.source: canfornav.com/fleet · vesselfinder.com IMO 9413913
facts: Canfornav names its whole fleet after ducks — this one too
The maccoa she's named for is a stiff-tailed diving duck from Africa.

vessels.name: OAKGLEN
vessels.fact: 730 ft Seaway-max bulker, built 1980 — a CSL 'glen' ship
vessels.source: cslships.com/vessel/oakglen
facts: 730 ft Seaway-max bulker, built 1980 — a CSL 'glen' ship
She was built in 1980 by Cockerill Yards in Hoboken, Belgium.
She began life as an ocean-going saltie named Federal Danube.
She sailed as Lake Ontario before Canada Steamship Lines renamed her Oakglen in 2009.

vessels.name: SAMUEL RISLEY
vessels.fact: Icebreaker that can chew through 2 ft of Great Lakes ice
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CCGS_Samuel_Risley
facts: Icebreaker that can chew through 2 ft of Great Lakes ice
She's named for Samuel Risley, Upper Canada's first chief steamship inspector.
She was built in 1985 on the west coast, in Delta, British Columbia.
Besides breaking ice, she also services and replaces navigation buoys.
She keeps an ice-free channel open between Port Colborne and Thunder Bay.

vessels.name: IVER BRIGHT
vessels.fact: Dutch-flag bitumen tanker hauling hot liquid asphalt
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 9616759
facts: Dutch-flag bitumen tanker hauling hot liquid asphalt
She was built in 2012 at the Hyundai Mipo shipyard in Ulsan, South Korea.
She was built to ice-class standards so she can work cold-weather routes.
She has a sister tanker named Iver Brilliant, built at the same Korean yard.

vessels.name: MCASPHALT ADVANTAGE
vessels.fact: New in 2024 — keeps its cargo heated so it stays liquid
vessels.source: shipfax.blogspot.com/2025/09/mcasphalt-advantage-first-timer.html
facts: New in 2024 — keeps its cargo heated so it stays liquid
She was designed in Sweden by FKAB and built at China's Wuhu Shipyard.
Her twin dual-fuel engines can run on cleaner liquefied natural gas to cut emissions.
Separate onboard tanks let her carry both bitumen and asphalt at once.
A full battery and UPS system keeps her powered to prevent sudden blackouts.

vessels.name: ALGOMA ENDEAVOUR
vessels.fact: Delivered 2025 — one of Algoma's newest Seaway-max lakers
vessels.source: algonet.com/ship/algoma-endeavour/
facts: Delivered 2025 — one of Algoma's newest Seaway-max lakers
She was built at the 3. Maj shipyard in Rijeka, Croatia.
She is the twelfth and final ship in Algoma's Equinox class.
Her Equinox design burns less fuel, cutting carbon intensity about forty percent versus older ships.

vessels.name: FEDERAL SAKURA
vessels.fact: Japanese-built 2005 saltie sailing for Montreal's Fednav
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 9288291 — built Shin Kurushima Onishi, Japan; owner Fednav, Montreal; LOA 190.44 m
facts: Japanese-built 2005 saltie sailing for Montreal's Fednav
Her name, Sakura, is the Japanese word for cherry blossom.
She was built by the Shin Kurushima shipyard in Onishi, Japan.
A Fednav fleetmate built the same year at the same Japanese yard carries the matching name Federal Katsura.
She can carry roughly thirty-two thousand tonnes of cargo.

vessels.name: JAMES J. VERSLUIS
vessels.fact: Chicago's ice-crushing tug — smashing lake ice since 1957
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_J._Versluis; WBEZ Chicago — 90 ft, built 1957 Sturgeon Bay, breaks 18 in of ice
facts: Chicago's ice-crushing tug — smashing lake ice since 1957
She is named for a Chicago water-works engineer who served the city four decades.
She was built in 1957 at Sturgeon Bay Shipbuilding in Wisconsin.
Her main job is clearing ice around Chicago's offshore water-intake cribs.

vessels.name: MUNTGRACHT
vessels.fact: Spliethoff cargo ship · 3 cranes, biggest lifting 80 tons
vessels.source: scheepvaartwest.be IMO 9571545 — cranes 80/65/50 t, LOA 142.1 m. CORRECTED: built 2009 at Zhoushan, China, not 2012
facts: Spliethoff cargo ship · 3 cranes, biggest lifting 80 tons
Spliethoff names all its ships after Dutch canals, called grachten.
She was built for Spliethoff at a shipyard in Zhoushan, China.
Fourteen removable steel deck pontoons let her reshape her holds for odd-shaped cargo.
She can also carry over three hundred refrigerated shipping containers.

vessels.name: DETROIT PRINCESS
vessels.fact: Ex-casino boat from 1993 Louisiana · carries 1,900 guests
vessels.source: detroitprincess.com/page-about-1.php. CORRECTED: NOT a paddlewheeler (two Cummins diesels); deck count not supported by official source
facts: Ex-casino boat from 1993 Louisiana · carries 1,900 guests
She started life as the Players Riverboat Casino Two.
Too big for the Mississippi, she was towed around Florida to reach Detroit.
At 222 feet, she is billed as America's second-largest riverboat.
She holds thirty thousand square feet of dining and event space.

vessels.name: J.S.ST.JOHN
vessels.fact: Built 1945 as US Navy oiler YO-178 · now a sand dredger
vessels.source: greatlakes.bgsu.edu/item/441100 — built 1945 Pensacola FL as USS YO-178, converted to sandsucker 1951, renamed J.S. St. John 1967; 51 m
facts: Built 1945 as US Navy oiler YO-178 · now a sand dredger
She was built far from the lakes, down in Pensacola, Florida.
Before the Great Lakes she sailed as a tanker named Lake Edward.
She is the last of the old sandsuckers still working the Great Lakes.
She was rebuilt from a Navy fuel tanker into a sand dredge at Erie.

vessels.name: BURNS HARBOR
vessels.fact: 1,000 ft long · hauls 80,900 tons of coal or iron ore
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Burns_Harbor. CORRECTED: 80,900 dwt at midsummer draft; the '78,850 tons in seven holds' claim was not supported
facts: 1,000 ft long · hauls 80,900 tons of coal or iron ore
She is named for Bethlehem Steel's steel-making complex at Burns Harbor, Indiana.
Her 250-foot boom can unload cargo at ten thousand tons an hour.
She was the tenth thousand-footer ever to sail the Great Lakes.
She was Bethlehem Steel's third and last thousand-foot freighter.

vessels.name: INDIANA HARBOR
vessels.fact: 1,000-ft self-unloader built 1979 in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Indiana_Harbor. CORRECTED: 250-ft swinging boom claim unverifiable; replaced with confirmed build details
facts: 1,000-ft self-unloader built 1979 in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin
In 1982 she became the first U.S. laker with satellite communications.
Her unloading boom swings ninety-two degrees to discharge on either side.
She was the ninth thousand-footer built for the Great Lakes.
Her thirty-seven hatches feed seven holds carrying nearly seventy-nine thousand tons.

vessels.name: JOHN J. BOLAND
vessels.fact: Sailed as Charles E. Wilson until 2000 · 680 ft self-unloader
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_John_J._Boland — launched Mar 1973 as Charles E. Wilson, renamed Jan 2000; 680 ft; American Steamship Co
facts: Sailed as Charles E. Wilson until 2000 · 680 ft self-unloader
She was the first of ten ships American Steamship ordered from Bay Shipbuilding.
She was built in 1973 at Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin.
Her 250-foot boom lets her unload without any help from shore.

vessels.name: ROBERT S. PIERSON
vessels.fact: Sailed as Wolverine for 34 years · renamed Pierson in 2008
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Robert_S._Pierson. CORRECTED: launched Sept 1973 (maiden voyage 1974); 630 ft, not unknown
facts: Sailed as Wolverine for 34 years · renamed Pierson in 2008
She was the first ship in the Lower Lakes fleet ever named for a person.
Robert Scott Pierson founded his own shipping firm, the Soo River Company, in 1975.
She was built by American Ship Building in Lorain, Ohio, for about fourteen million dollars.
She's a compact river-class laker, built small enough to work up Cleveland's Cuyahoga River.

vessels.name: HERBERT C JACKSON
vessels.fact: Steam-powered for 57 years — went diesel in winter 2015-16
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Alpena (documents the winter 2015-16 conversion of Herbert C. Jackson and John G. Munson to diesel); VesselFinder (built 1959). 'Interlake's last steamer' could not be confirmed and was dropped.
facts: Steam-powered for 57 years — went diesel in winter 2015-16
She was the first laker to place her steam turbines forward of her boilers.
She's named for Herbert Cooper Jackson, an executive at Interlake's former parent company.
Converted to a self-unloader in 1975, she now discharges through a 250-foot boom.

vessels.name: GARDNO
vessels.fact: Built 2018 — 656 ft carrying 36,600 tons of cargo
vessels.source: VesselFinder IMO 9767704 (200 m LOA, 36,643 DWT, built 2018). Polsteam ownership and the '3 paying passengers' claim could NOT be verified — Polsteam's Wikipedia fleet list does not include Gardno and the flag is Bahamas; both dropped.
facts: Built 2018 — 656 ft carrying 36,600 tons of cargo
She's named after Lake Gardno, a coastal lake in northern Poland.
She arrived in 2018 with sisters Jamno and Narie, also named for Polish lakes.
Like her Polsteam fleetmates, she carries a handful of passengers across the ocean.

vessels.name: ALGOMA EQUINOX
vessels.fact: Lead ship of the Equinox class — 740 ft, built 2013 in China
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algoma_Equinox — confirms lead ship of her class, 225.6 m (740 ft 2 in), completed 25 Sep 2013 at Nantong Mingde Heavy Industries, China
facts: Lead ship of the Equinox class — 740 ft, built 2013 in China
She was built by Nantong Mingde Heavy Industries in Nantong, China.
She's far more fuel-efficient than her older fleetmates, and her scrubbers strip out 97 percent of her sulfur emissions.
This gearless carrier relies on shore-side equipment to unload her cargo.
She was launched on Christmas Eve, 2012, before crossing the Atlantic to Canada.

vessels.name: ALGOMA COMPASS
vessels.fact: First ship built in Toledo since 1959 — sailing since 1973
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algoma_Compass — explicitly states as Roger M. Kyes she 'marked the first ship to be constructed in Toledo since 1959'; launched 28 Mar 1973, completed 1 Aug 1973, 207.3 m
facts: First ship built in Toledo since 1959 — sailing since 1973
She first sailed as Roger M. Kyes, then Adam E. Cornelius, before becoming Algoma Compass.
Her 260-foot boom can unload cargo at nearly 6,000 tons an hour.
Her first namesake, Roger M. Kyes, was a General Motors executive and former U.S. Deputy Secretary of Defense who ran the American Steamship Company.

vessels.name: LAKE EXPRESS
vessels.fact: First high-speed car ferry on the Great Lakes — 192 ft, 2004
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HSC_Lake_Express — CORRECTED: it was only 'one of the first' high-speed auto ferries built in the US, but 'the first high-speed auto ferry to see service on the Great Lakes'. 191 ft 7 in, Austal USA, service began 1 Jun 2004.
facts: First high-speed car ferry on the Great Lakes — 192 ft, 2004
She was built by Austal USA in Mobile, Alabama.
Four waterjets drive her across the lake at up to 34 knots, about 39 miles per hour.
She crosses Lake Michigan between Milwaukee and Muskegon in about two and a half hours.
She carries up to 248 passengers along with 44 cars and a dozen motorcycles.

vessels.name: MANITOULIN
vessels.fact: Lower Lakes self-unloader — 1991 hull, 663 ft, 27,550 tons
vessels.source: VesselFinder (self-discharging bulk carrier, built 1991, 202 m, 27,550 DWT); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Lakes_Towing (fleet member). The 'new bow welded to an old tanker's stern in 2015' story could NOT be sourced from any reachable reference and was dropped.
facts: Lower Lakes self-unloader — 1991 hull, 663 ft, 27,550 tons
She began life in 1991 as the oil tanker Trelsi, built in Croatia.
In 2015 her tanker bow was replaced with a new self-unloading forebody in China.
Before her rebuild she also sailed as Euro Swan and Lalandia Swan.
She's named for Manitoulin Island, the largest freshwater island in the world.

vessels.name: ALGOMA INNOVATOR
vessels.fact: Algoma River Class self-unloader, 2018 — 24,454 DWT
vessels.source: algonet.com/fleet/algoma-innovator/ — CORRECTED build year to 2018 (Algoma lists built and delivered 2018, not 2017); River Class, 24,454 MT DWT, Canadian flag. Forward-mounted boom claim and 650 ft length could not be verified and were dropped.
facts: Algoma River Class self-unloader, 2018 — 24,454 DWT
She was built in Croatia by the Uljanik shipbuilding group.
Her unloading boom is mounted forward, letting her reach tighter, harder-to-serve docks.
She was hailed as the most efficient river-class laker in nearly 40 years.
In 2018 she made her maiden trans-Atlantic voyage from Croatia to Canada.

vessels.name: USEPA LAKE GUARDIAN
vessels.fact: Largest research vessel on the Great Lakes — 180 ft floating lab
vessels.source: epa.gov/great-lakes-monitoring/lake-guardian — EPA states it is 'the largest research vessel operating on the Great Lakes', 180 feet, 959 gross tons. Build year not stated on the page; left as unknown.
facts: Largest research vessel on the Great Lakes — 180 ft floating lab
She carries three onboard labs for wet work, chemistry, and biology.
She can host 27 scientists working alongside her crew of 14.

vessels.name: STRANDJA
vessels.fact: Ex-Federal Yangtze — 610 ft saltie built in 2010
vessels.source: VesselFinder IMO 9564140 (bulk carrier, built 2010, 186 m, Malta flag, ex-FEDERAL YANGTZE, ex-EASTWIND YORK). Bulgarian operator and mountain-range naming could NOT be verified (Navibulgar site unreachable) and were dropped.
facts: Ex-Federal Yangtze — 610 ft saltie built in 2010

vessels.name: DIRK S. VANENKEVORT
vessels.fact: Built from leftover steel of the Joseph H. Thompson conversion
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Marine_Robin — CORRECTED: the tug was 'constructed from leftover steel from the barge conversion', NOT from the cut-off stern; renamed from Joseph H. Thompson Jr. during a Donjon (Erie, PA) refit. Build year 1990 and 125 ft length could not be confirmed and were zeroed.
facts: Built from leftover steel of the Joseph H. Thompson conversion
She began her career back in 1990 as the tug Joseph H. Thompson Jr.
A major 2020 rebuild by DonJon in Erie, Pennsylvania gave her this new name.
Her engines push the 740-foot self-unloading barge Michigan Trader.
She was the very first ship through the Soo Locks to open the 2026 season.

vessels.name: SAM LAUD
vessels.fact: Bay Shipbuilding 1975 — hauls 24,300 tons a trip
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Sam_Laud — CORRECTED: launched 1975 and in service April 1975, not 1974; the 'side-launched' detail is not stated by any source found. 634 ft 10 in, Bay Shipbuilding Sturgeon Bay, 24,300 tons at midsummer draft (confirmed).
facts: Bay Shipbuilding 1975 — hauls 24,300 tons a trip

vessels.name: FEDERAL FRASER
vessels.fact: Built 2021 — 656 ft, 34,492 tons deadweight
vessels.source: VesselFinder IMO 9866744 (bulk carrier, built 2021, 199.98 m, 34,492 DWT, Marshall Islands flag). Japanese shipyard (Oshima) could not be independently confirmed — fednav.com returned 403 — so that detail was dropped.
facts: Built 2021 — 656 ft, 34,492 tons deadweight
She sails under the Marshall Islands flag for Montreal-based Fednav.
Her owner Fednav boasts the world's largest fleet of ice-class bulk carriers.

vessels.name: PATRICIAHOEY
vessels.fact: Built 1949 · 2,000 hp tug still working the Detroit River
vessels.source: tugboatinformation.com/tug.cfm?id=5909, gltugs.wordpress.com/patricia-hoey/
facts: Built 1949 · 2,000 hp tug still working the Detroit River
She was launched way back in 1949 in New Orleans under the name Propeller.
For decades she towed along the Texas Gulf coast before heading north.
Detroit's Gaelic Tugboat Company rebuilt her and renamed her Bantry Bay in 1982.
Today she refuels other ships as a hardworking bunkering tug.

vessels.name: STENHEIM
vessels.fact: Portuguese-flagged chemical tanker, 472 ft, built 2003
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com/vessels/details/9261114 (flag Portugal/Madeira, 144 m, 2003)
facts: Portuguese-flagged chemical tanker, 472 ft, built 2003
Norway's Stenersen line manages her, and every Stenersen ship carries a 'Sten' name.
Her epoxy-coated tanks let her carry many different chemical cargoes.
She can carry roughly 16,600 tonnes of liquid cargo.

vessels.name: CITY OF ALGONAC
vessels.fact: Crosses the US–Canada border in about 10 minutes
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walpole–Algonac_Ferry (built 1990, 8-10 min crossing)
facts: Crosses the US–Canada border in about 10 minutes
She links Algonac, Michigan with Walpole Island, Ontario across the St. Clair River.
The little ferry carries up to twelve cars on each short crossing.
Today she is the only ferry still operating between Michigan and Ontario.
Ferry service on this crossing dates back at least to 1922.

vessels.name: GL OSTRANDER
vessels.fact: Tug + barge Integrity = 544-ft cement-hauling combo
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/g-l-ostrander/, tugboatinformation.com/tug.cfm?id=1430
facts: Tug + barge Integrity = 544-ft cement-hauling combo
Before her current name she also sailed as Robert L. Torres and Jacklyn M.
She has been repowered twice and now makes 7,200 horsepower.
She pushes the cement barge Integrity as an articulated tug, managed by Andrie Incorporated.

vessels.name: RT HON PAUL J MARTIN
vessels.fact: Built 1973 as H.M. Griffith · 740-ft self-unloader
vessels.source: cslships.com/vessel/rt-hon-paul-j-martin/ (225.50 m = 740 ft; 738 was wrong), greatlakesships.wordpress.com/h-m-griffith/
facts: Built 1973 as H.M. Griffith · 740-ft self-unloader
She's named for Paul Martin Senior, a cabinet minister and father of a prime minister.
She was built at the Collingwood shipyard in Ontario.
A 2000 rebuild gave her a new bow built to the maximum Seaway dimensions.

vessels.name: MESABI MINER
vessels.fact: 1,004 ft — built in three pieces at two shipyards
vessels.source: interlake-steamship.com, doorcountypulse.com (midbody Toledo, assembled Lorain, American Shipbuilding)
facts: 1,004 ft — built in three pieces at two shipyards
She's too big for the Welland Canal, so she stays on the upper lakes.
Even at a thousand feet, she can maneuver in harbor without tugboat help.
Her fleetmates include the giants James R. Barker and Paul R. Tregurtha.

vessels.name: EVANS SPIRIT
vessels.fact: Dutch-built 2007 · designed for shallow-draft Lakes ports
vessels.source: mckeil.com/our-fleet/evans-spirit/ (bulk/breakbulk, shallow draft — aluminum-slab claim NOT verifiable, removed); built Niestern Sander, Delfzijl NL
facts: Dutch-built 2007 · designed for shallow-draft Lakes ports
She first sailed in 2007 as the Italian cargo ship Spavalda.
Canada's McKeil Marine bought her in 2017 and gave her this name.
She's now Canadian-flagged and sails for Hamilton-based McKeil Marine.
Two roomy holds let her carry about 15,000 tonnes of cargo.

vessels.name: BAIE COMEAU
vessels.fact: Built in China, 2013 — sailed across the Pacific to the Lakes
vessels.source: boatnerd.com/pictures/fleet/BaieComeau.htm (Chengxi Shipyard, delivered 20 Jun 2013, departed China 30 Jun)
facts: Built in China, 2013 — sailed across the Pacific to the Lakes
She was the fourth and last Trillium-class self-unloader built for Canada Steamship Lines.
She's named for Baie-Comeau, Quebec, whose mayor was presented with a nearly eight-foot scale model of the ship.
Her self-unloading gear can pour out cargo at about 5,450 tonnes every hour.

vessels.name: ALGOCANADA
vessels.fact: Built 2008 · 426-ft tanker hauling petroleum on the Lakes
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com/vessels/details/9378591 (129.84 m = 426 ft, 2008, Canadian-flag chem/oil products tanker)
facts: Built 2008 · 426-ft tanker hauling petroleum on the Lakes
She's a double-hulled tanker, built after new rules banned single-hulled tankers from the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence Seaway.

vessels.name: WALTER J MCCARTHY
vessels.fact: First 1,000-footer built at Bay Shipbuilding, 1977
vessels.source: doorcountypulse.com (superlative explicitly confirmed), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Walter_J._McCarthy_Jr.
facts: First 1,000-footer built at Bay Shipbuilding, 1977
She first sailed as the Belle River, renamed in 1990 for a retired chairman of Detroit Edison.
Her hull was built in two sections, then welded together in the shipyard's drydock.
She entered service in 1977, hauling coal to a Detroit Edison power plant.

vessels.name: THUNDER BAY
vessels.fact: CSL Trillium-class laker — built in China, delivered 2013
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trillium-class_freighter (Chengxi Shipyard, Jiangyin; delivered 16 May 2013), cslships.com/vessel/thunder-bay/ (225.50 m)
facts: CSL Trillium-class laker — built in China, delivered 2013
Named for the Port of Thunder Bay, she paid a call on her namesake city in 2013.
Her unloading conveyor rides a long boom that can swing out over either side.
She revived the name of an earlier CSL 'Bay'-series freighter built back in 1952.

vessels.name: MARK W. BARKER
vessels.fact: First new US-built laker in nearly 40 years · 639 ft
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Mark_W._Barker; interlake-steamship.com — first US-flagged Great Lakes bulk carrier built since 1983
facts: First new US-built laker in nearly 40 years · 639 ft
She's named after Interlake Steamship's own president, Mark W. Barker.
She's the first ship on the Great Lakes powered by cleaner EPA Tier 4 engines.
Her unloading boom was salvaged from the scrapped steamer American Victory.
She's built to carry unusual cargo like wind-turbine blades on deck.

vessels.name: KAYE E BARKER
vessels.fact: 1952 · first lake freighter built entirely in drydock
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Kaye_E._Barker — built as SS Edward B. Greene, first laker built from keel up in drydock (Toledo)
facts: 1952 · first lake freighter built entirely in drydock
She was launched as the Edward B. Greene and later renamed Benson Ford.
Her current name honors Kaye Barker, wife of an Interlake Steamship president.
In the mid-1970s she was lengthened by 120 feet to carry more ore.
She was converted in 1981 to unload herself with a 250-foot deck boom.

vessels.name: G3 MARQUIS
vessels.fact: 740-ft Equinox-class grain hauler, built 2014
vessels.source: boatnerd.com/pictures/fleet/G3Marquis.htm; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equinox-class_freighter — launched 8 Jul 2014, 740x78
facts: 740-ft Equinox-class grain hauler, built 2014
She first sailed as CWB Marquis for the Canadian Wheat Board.
She was built at the Nantong Mingde shipyard in China.
Exhaust scrubbers strip about 97 percent of the sulphur out of her emissions.
She's named after Marquis wheat, a Canadian variety so successful that 20 million acres were planted within a decade of its release.

vessels.name: JOSEPH L BLOCK
vessels.fact: 1976 · first diesel ship in the Inland Steel fleet
vessels.source: greatlakesvesselhistory.com; greatlakesships.wordpress.com/joseph-l-block — christened 29 Jun 1976, first diesel in Inland Steel fleet
facts: 1976 · first diesel ship in the Inland Steel fleet
Launched at Sturgeon Bay in 1976, she spent decades hauling iron ore out of Escanaba.

vessels.name: JOHN G MUNSON
vessels.fact: World's largest self-unloader when built in 1952
vessels.source: greatlakesvesselhistory.com Munson John G. 2 — explicitly the largest self-unloader in the world when built; lengthened 1976
facts: World's largest self-unloader when built in 1952
Built at Manitowoc, Wisconsin, she became flagship of the Bradley Transportation fleet.
She's named for John G. Munson, a limestone-company president who became a vice president of U.S. Steel.
She was lengthened by 102 feet in 1976 to carry even more cargo.
Her original steam power gave way to a modern diesel engine in 2016.

vessels.name: EXEBORG
vessels.fact: Dutch saltwater trader — built 2013 · 474 ft
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 9650482 — 144.56 m (474 ft), Netherlands flag, general cargo, built 2013. Length corrected from 476 to 474.
facts: Dutch saltwater trader — built 2013 · 474 ft
She was built at the Royal Niestern Sander yard in Delfzijl, the Netherlands.
Four removable tween-decks let her reshape her holds for very different cargoes.
Her strengthened holds are built to carry heavy, oversized project cargo.

vessels.name: PETIT FORTE
vessels.fact: Canadian pusher tug working the lakes since 1969
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 6826119 — pusher tug, built 1969, Canada flag. CORRECTED: original claim that it pushes the barge 'St. Marys Cement' could NOT be verified and was removed.
facts: Canadian pusher tug working the lakes since 1969
She was built in 1969 in Selby, England, by Cochrane and Sons.
She has carried five different names, first sailing as the E. Bronson Ingram.
Before crossing to the Lakes she worked overseas as the Al Battal.
Today she pushes the cement barge St. Marys Cement, registered in Hamilton, Ontario.

vessels.name: ALPENA
vessels.fact: Built 1942 — oldest active freighter on the Great Lakes
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Alpena_(1942); glc.org/dailynews/20250829-oldest-freighter — 519 ft after 1989 shortening
facts: Built 1942 — oldest active freighter on the Great Lakes
She launched in 1942 with the largest cargo capacity of any ship on the Lakes.
One of five identical wartime ore carriers, she could haul enough iron ore to make the steel for eight destroyers.
In 1989 her 120-foot midsection was removed and she became a cement carrier.
She was built as the Leon Fraser at Ecorse, Michigan's Great Lakes Engineering Works.

vessels.name: CSL TADOUSSAC
vessels.fact: Last CSL laker built with the classic bow bridge
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSL_Tadoussac — 'the last freighter built for CSL in the traditional two superstructure design, which puts her bridge up in the ship's bow'
facts: Last CSL laker built with the classic bow bridge
She was the first Canada Steamship Lines ship built with her self-unloading gear mounted aft.
She was built at the Collingwood Shipyards on Ontario's Georgian Bay.

vessels.name: AMERICAN MARINER
vessels.fact: 1980 self-unloader with a 250-ft stern boom · 730 ft
vessels.source: greatlakesships.wordpress.com/american-mariner — 730 ft LOA, 1980, aft-mounted 250-ft boom. CORRECTED: the '6,000 tons an hour' rate is NOT published for this vessel (that figure belongs to Joseph L. Block) and was removed.
facts: 1980 self-unloader with a 250-ft stern boom · 730 ft
She was built at Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin.
She was nearly named Chicago before she launched as the American Mariner.
Her seven cargo holds are filled through twenty-four deck hatches.

vessels.name: AMERICAN PATRIOT
vessels.fact: Sails all-American cruises across the Great Lakes
vessels.source: americancruiselines.com press release; travelweekly.com — 'first all-U.S.' rests on operator's own claim, echoed by trade press; length not verified
facts: Sails all-American cruises across the Great Lakes
She was built in 2025 by Chesapeake Shipbuilding in Salisbury, Maryland.
She's an intimate small ship, carrying just 130 guests across five decks.
She's the very first of American Cruise Lines' new Patriot Class.
She entered service in June 2025, debuting on a New England cruise from Boston.

vessels.name: CSL ST-LAURENT
vessels.fact: Trillium Class laker built in China — 740 ft long
vessels.source: Wikipedia Trillium-class freighter (225.5 m / 739 ft 10 in, Yangfan Shipyard, Zhoushan, China, 2014); cslships.com spec sheet
facts: Trillium Class laker built in China — 740 ft long
She was the last of CSL's Trillium Class ships built.
Her delivery voyage from China to Montreal took roughly two months.

vessels.name: CSL LAURENTIEN
vessels.fact: Sailing since 1977 — rebuilt as a self-unloader in 2001
vessels.source: cslships.com/vessel/csl-laurentien — built 1977, converted to self-unloader 2001, LOA 225.48 m, ex-Louis R. Desmarais. NOTE: original 'whole new forebody' wording dropped — CSL documents a self-unloader conversion, not a forebody swap
facts: Sailing since 1977 — rebuilt as a self-unloader in 2001
She first sailed as the Louis R. Desmarais, named for a Canada Steamship Lines president.
Her 2000 rebuild grafted a brand-new bow and cargo section onto her original stern.
She was built at the Collingwood Shipyards, fourth of five sister ships.

vessels.name: DOROTHY ANN
vessels.fact: 124-ft Z-drive tug — pushing barge Pathfinder since 1999
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com (pusher tug, 1999, 38 m = 124 ft); Wikipedia Interlake Steamship Company + J. L. Mauthe. CORRECTED: barge Pathfinder is 647 ft, not 700 ft, and the pair is an ARTICULATED tug-barge, not a rigid unit — both errors removed
facts: 124-ft Z-drive tug — pushing barge Pathfinder since 1999
She's the largest Z-drive tug ever built in North America, at 7,200 horsepower.
Her twin drives let her spin on her own axis and stop within her own length.
Her barge Pathfinder was rebuilt from a 1950s lake freighter, the J.L. Mauthe.
She was built at Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin.

vessels.name: CALUMET
vessels.fact: Built 1973 as William R. Roesch — still hauling at 630 ft
vessels.source: Wikipedia Calumet (1973 ship) — 630 ft, built 1973 by American Ship Building, Lorain OH, ex-William R. Roesch, still in service
facts: Built 1973 as William R. Roesch — still hauling at 630 ft
She was built at the American Shipbuilding Company in Lorain, Ohio.
She sailed as the David Z. Norton from 1995 until 2006.
Her aft-mounted self-unloading boom stretches 260 feet.
She's a compact 'River-class' self-unloader, built to reach docks up tight waterways like the Cuyahoga River.

vessels.name: FEDERAL BISCAY
vessels.fact: Ocean-going salty — 656 ft, 34,500 tons deadweight
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 9697856 — 2015, 199.98 m (656 ft), 34,564 DWT. NOTE: 'built in Japan' removed, could not be confirmed
facts: Ocean-going salty — 656 ft, 34,500 tons deadweight
She was built in 2015 by Oshima Shipbuilding in Japan.
She's operated by Montreal-based Fednav as one of its Seaway-size 'laker' bulk carriers.

vessels.name: AMERICAN CENTURY
vessels.fact: A 1,000-footer — carries 80,900 tons of ore or coal
vessels.source: Wikipedia MV American Century — 1,000 ft, built 1981 Bay Shipbuilding, 80,900 tons at midsummer draft, ex-Columbia Star
facts: A 1,000-footer — carries 80,900 tons of ore or coal
She was the very last of the thousand-footers to enter service on the Lakes.
She began life as the Columbia Star, taking the name American Century in 2006.
She was built at Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin, back in 1981.
Four diesel engines give her about fourteen thousand horsepower to move enormous cargoes.

vessels.name: KAREN ANDRIE
vessels.fact: Pusher tug working the Lakes since 1965 — 112 ft
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com — pusher tug, built 1965, 34 m (112 ft), 458 GT, in service. CORRECTED: 'Texas-built' and the barge Endeavour pairing could not be confirmed and were removed
facts: Pusher tug working the Lakes since 1965 — 112 ft
She was built down in Texas in 1965, first named the Sarah Hays.
For years she handled dry-bulk barges out of Tampa, Florida.
Andrie Inc. of Muskegon, Michigan bought her and gave her this name in 1993.
A 2009 refit gave her a new upper pilothouse and a JAK coupler to lock onto the barge Endeavour.

vessels.name: WILFRED SYKES
vessels.fact: Queen of the Lakes 1949-52 — first streamlined laker
vessels.source: Wikipedia Queen of the Lakes — held title 28 Jun 1949 to Nov 1952, succeeded by Joseph H. Thompson, noted as first streamlined design. NOTE: 'still sailing after 75 years' removed — current operating status not confirmed
facts: Queen of the Lakes 1949-52 — first streamlined laker
She is considered the first of the modern Great Lakes freighters.
She was named for Wilfred Sykes, who became president of Inland Steel in 1948.
When she was rebuilt as a self-unloader at Superior, Wisconsin in 1975, she was the first laker with the unloading gear mounted aft.

vessels.name: BBC KOLDING
vessels.fact: Brand-new general cargo ship — launched in 2026
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 9964479 — general cargo, built 2026, 149 m (489 ft). NOTE: 'one of the newest on the Lakes' was an unverifiable inference and was removed
facts: Brand-new general cargo ship — launched in 2026
She belongs to BBC Chartering's new LakerMax class, a run of fifteen heavy-lift ships the company began introducing in 2024.

vessels.name: ALGOSOLIS
vessels.fact: Product tanker that joined Algoma's Canadian fleet in 2024
vessels.source: algonet.com/ship/algosolis (built 2009, delivered to Algoma 2024, 16,544 DWT); vesselfinder.com IMO 9409261 = 144.1 m LOA, built 2009, Jiangnan Shipyard, Algoma Tankers Ltd
facts: Product tanker that joined Algoma's Canadian fleet in 2024
Before Algoma, she sailed as the Eli Knutsen for a Norwegian owner.
She carries roughly sixteen thousand tons of liquid petroleum products.

vessels.name: CLYDE S. VANENKEVORT
vessels.fact: Tug that pushes the 740-ft self-unloading barge Erie Trader
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/clyde-s-vanenkevort — built 2011 by DonJon Shipbuilding, Erie PA as KEN BOOTHE SR., 135 ft 4 in, renamed 2017; vtbarge.com fleet page + NTSB MAB1912 confirm Erie Trader 740 ft, 2012. CORRECTED: input said built 2008 / 130 ft
facts: Tug that pushes the 740-ft self-unloading barge Erie Trader
She was built in Erie, Pennsylvania, and first named the Ken Boothe Senior.
VanEnkevort Tug and Barge bought her and gave her this name in 2017.
Her two engines produce nearly eleven thousand horsepower to drive the barge.

vessels.name: VERILA
vessels.fact: Handysize bulk carrier, Malta-flagged, brand new in 2022
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com vessel search VERILA — bulk carrier, built 2022, 32,165 DWT, 190 x 24 m; vesseltracker.com IMO 9905734, MMSI 229656000 / callsign 9HA5549 = Malta flag. CORRECTED: could NOT verify 'Bulgarian' flag (Malta-flagged) or the ice-class / 'built for winter Seaway runs' claim — Seaway closes in winter, so that claim was dropped
facts: Handysize bulk carrier, Malta-flagged, brand new in 2022
She shares her name with Verila, a mountain range in western Bulgaria.

vessels.name: PEARL MIST
vessels.fact: Finished in 2010 — lawsuits delayed her debut until 2014
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl_Mist — completed June 2010 at Halifax Shipyards, 99.1 m (325 ft 2 in), 210 passengers, legal battles settled after 2013 appeals ruling, maiden voyage June 2014
facts: Finished in 2010 — lawsuits delayed her debut until 2014
She was built by Irving's Halifax Shipyard in Nova Scotia, Canada.
She carries up to two hundred ten guests with about seventy crew.
She was ordered for around forty-three million dollars back in 2006.
In 2023 she received a full, top-to-bottom interior makeover.

vessels.name: ALGOMA STRONGFIELD
vessels.fact: 740 ft — the biggest that fits the Welland Canal locks
vessels.source: algonet.com/ship/algoma-strongfield — built 2017, class listed as 'Seaway Max', 30,303 DWT; 740 ft is the maximum permitted Seaway/Welland lock length (225.5 m)
facts: 740 ft — the biggest that fits the Welland Canal locks
She was first ordered as the CWB Strongfield by the Canadian Wheat Board.
Algoma bought her unfinished at auction after the Chinese shipyard went bankrupt.
Her exhaust scrubbers remove about ninety-seven percent of sulphur oxide emissions.

vessels.name: SAMUEL DE CHAMPLAIN
vessels.fact: Built 1976 as an ocean tug — now pushes cement on the Lakes
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_de_Champlain_(tugboat) — built 1976 by Mangone Shipbuilding, Houston as MUSKETEER FURY for a Norwegian owner (ocean tug), 140 ft; bought by Lafarge 2006, paired with 460-ft cement barge INNOVATION
facts: Built 1976 as an ocean tug — now pushes cement on the Lakes
She was built in Houston, Texas, and first named the Musketeer Fury.
She survived a serious fire off the Azores in 1993 before being rebuilt.
She sailed under six different names during her long career.

vessels.name: ARTHUR M ANDERSON
vessels.fact: Last ship to speak with the Edmund Fitzgerald, 1975
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Arthur_M._Anderson — launched 1952, originally 647 ft, lengthened to 767 ft winter 1974-75; explicitly 'the last ship to be in contact with SS Edmund Fitzgerald before she sank on November 10, 1975' and first rescue vessel on scene
facts: Last ship to speak with the Edmund Fitzgerald, 1975
After the Fitzgerald vanished, she turned back into the storm at the Coast Guard's request to search for survivors.
She's named for Arthur Marvin Anderson, a U.S. Steel director and vice chairman of J.P. Morgan and Company.
The American Ship Building Company launched her at Lorain, Ohio, in February 1952.
A new 120-foot midsection added in 1975 stretched her to 767 feet.

vessels.name: CASON J CALLAWAY
vessels.fact: Built 1952 · stretched 120 ft longer in 1974
vessels.source: greatlakesships.wordpress.com/cason-j-callaway — built 1952, 'Lengthened by 120', Fraser Shipyards, Superior, Wisconsin, 1974', 647 ft to 767 ft
facts: Built 1952 · stretched 120 ft longer in 1974
She honors Cason Callaway, a Georgia textile magnate who created the famed Callaway Gardens.
She was built at the Great Lakes Engineering Works in River Rouge, Michigan.
Fraser Shipyards rebuilt her as a self-unloader at Superior, Wisconsin, in 1982.

vessels.name: PHILIP R CLARKE
vessels.fact: First of the eight AAA-class lake freighters, built 1952
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Lakes_Fleet — 'First vessel of the AAA Class ore carriers'; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Arthur_M._Anderson calls Anderson 'second of eight of the AAA class', confirming the class size of 8. REWORDED: original said 'eight 1952 AAA class' but the class was built 1952-53, not all in 1952
facts: First of the eight AAA-class lake freighters, built 1952
Her keel was laid in December 1950 at American Shipbuilding in Lorain, Ohio.
Her AAA class used an asymmetrical stern to smooth water flow to the propeller.

vessels.name: STEWART J CORT
vessels.fact: First 1,000-footer on the Lakes — wears a big #1 aft
vessels.source: interlake-steamship.com/our-fleet/m-v-stewart-j-cort — 'the first 1000-foot vessel on the Great Lakes when she entered service for Bethlehem Steel in 1972'; 1,000 x 105 ft; 'She has a #1 painted on her aft house, a nod to her legacy of being the first thousand footer on the Lakes'
facts: First 1,000-footer on the Lakes — wears a big #1 aft
Her bow and stern were built in Mississippi, then joined to a mid-body built in Erie, Pennsylvania.
Before her mid-body arrived, the stubby bow-and-stern unit was nicknamed Stubby.
She's the only thousand-footer with her pilothouse mounted forward in the bow.

vessels.name: ROGER BLOUGH
vessels.fact: 858 ft — a construction fire delayed her 1972 debut a year
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Roger_Blough — 858 ft, American Ship Building, Lorain OH; June 24, 1971 engine room fire killed four, pushed the July 1971 launch to service entry June 1972. CAUTION for live use: laid up at Conneaut, OH since Oct 2022 — an AIS contact near the Straits under this name is likely spurious
facts: 858 ft — a construction fire delayed her 1972 debut a year
She's named for Roger Blough, a former chairman of U.S. Steel.
Her unusual aft shuttle boom slides cargo out through small openings in her stern.
The American Ship Building Company built her at its Lorain, Ohio, yard.

vessels.name: JAMES R BARKER
vessels.fact: First 1,000-footer built entirely on the Great Lakes
vessels.source: interlake-steamship.com (owner), duluth-ships wiki, Duluth News Tribune — superlative confirmed: first 1,000-ft class vessel built entirely on the Lakes, American Ship Building, Lorain OH, 1976
facts: First 1,000-footer built entirely on the Great Lakes
She's named for James R. Barker, chairman of the Interlake Steamship Company.
She was the third thousand-footer built for the Great Lakes.
Her deckhouse was built in Chicago and shipped to Lorain on the deck of another vessel.

vessels.name: MICHIPICOTEN
vessels.fact: Built 1952 · survived a 13-ft hull crack in 2024
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michipicoten_(1952_ship), NOAA IncidentNews #10799, gcaptain.com — LOA corrected from 698 to 683 ft (Wikipedia, post-1957 lengthening); USCG press used a rounded 690 ft
facts: Built 1952 · survived a 13-ft hull crack in 2024
She was launched in 1952 at Sparrows Point, Maryland, as the Elton Hoyt 2nd.
She reached the Lakes towed up the rivers, her cabins carried on deck and assembled in Chicago.
Her name means Big Bluffs in Ojibwe, after a river in Ontario.
Around 2010 to 2011 she was repowered from a steam turbine to a modern diesel engine.

vessels.name: H LEE WHITE
vessels.fact: Built 1974 · carries 35,400 tons at midsummer draft
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_H._Lee_White, greatlakesships.wordpress.com — REPLACED prior fact: the '6,000 tons per hour' unload rate appears only on fan wikis, not in Wikipedia or Shipwatcher specs; could not confirm, so dropped
facts: Built 1974 · carries 35,400 tons at midsummer draft
She's named for Harris Lee White, a former American Steamship Company chairman.
Bay Shipbuilding built her at Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin, in 1974.

vessels.name: BUFFALO
vessels.fact: Built 1978 · sails today as the Algoma Buffalo
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Buffalo — built 1978 Bay Shipbuilding, 634 ft 10 in LOA, bought by Algoma late 2017 and renamed Algoma Buffalo in 2018; a live 'BUFFALO' AIS hit is likely stale
facts: Built 1978 · sails today as the Algoma Buffalo
Bay Shipbuilding built her at Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin, for about 25 million dollars.
She slid into the water sideways in a dramatic 1978 side-launch.
She was one of ten sisters built under a 1970s U.S. maritime-aid program.

vessels.name: ADAM E CORNELIUS
vessels.fact: Built 1973 · renamed Algoma Compass in 2018
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algoma_Compass — built 1973, originally Roger M. Kyes, renamed Adam E. Cornelius 1989, Algoma Compass 2018; LOA 680 ft 1 in
facts: Built 1973 · renamed Algoma Compass in 2018
She first sailed as the Roger M. Kyes before becoming Adam E. Cornelius in 1989.
Built in Toledo, Ohio, she was the first ship constructed at that yard since 1959.
She was among the first Lakes freighters built with all crew quarters set aft.

vessels.name: ALGOMA CONVEYOR
vessels.fact: Its hull was bought at auction after the yard went bust
vessels.source: greatlakesships.wordpress.com/algoma-conveyor — hull started at Nantong Mingde (bankrupt), acquired by Algoma at auction, completed at Yangzijiang; 740 ft LOA
facts: Its hull was bought at auction after the yard went bust
She was the first Equinox-class self-unloader built for Algoma Central.
She sailed home from China across the Pacific and through the Panama Canal.
Her loop-belt system feeds a stern unloading boom over 260 feet long.

vessels.name: ALGOMA SAULT
vessels.fact: 740 ft — the maximum length the Seaway locks allow
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algoma_Sault — 740 ft LOA, Equinox-class, seawaymax. REWORDED: original 'the longest that fits' implied uniqueness; many lakers share the 740 ft Seaway max, so the superlative was softened to the limit itself
facts: 740 ft — the maximum length the Seaway locks allow
Her name is the third Algoma ship to honor Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario.
Her exhaust scrubber removes over 98 percent of the ship's sulfur-oxide emissions.
Her self-unloading boom reaches about 260 feet across the deck.

vessels.name: TIM S DOOL
vessels.fact: Built 1967 · widened in 1996, re-engined in 2007
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_S._Dool — launched 1967 as Senneville, beam widened at Port Weller Dry Docks 1996, re-engined with MaK 8M43C in 2007; 730 ft LOA
facts: Built 1967 · widened in 1996, re-engined in 2007
She was only the second laker ever built with a single stern superstructure.
She was built at Saint John, New Brunswick, a saltwater yard far from the Lakes.
She first sailed as Senneville, then Algoville, before taking her present name.
She's named for a former president of Algoma Central.

vessels.name: MANITOWOC
vessels.fact: Built 1973 · sailed first as the Paul Thayer
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Ship_Building_Company — CORRECTED: 'four different names' is wrong. Sources confirm only three: Paul Thayer (1973), Earl W. Oglebay (1994, Oglebay Norton), Manitowoc (2008, Lower Lakes). No source found for a separate 'Earl W.' name
facts: Built 1973 · sailed first as the Paul Thayer
She was built in Lorain, Ohio, by the American Shipbuilding Company.
Her present name honors the Manitowoc River in Wisconsin.
Earlier in her life she sailed as the Earl W. Oglebay.
Her very first job was hauling iron ore up Cleveland's Cuyahoga River.

vessels.name: VICTORY I
vessels.fact: Small-ship cruiser — visits all five Great Lakes, 202 guests
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victory_I; victorycruiselines.com/2026-voyage-calendar-2/
facts: Small-ship cruiser — visits all five Great Lakes, 202 guests
She was built in 2001 in Jacksonville, Florida, as the Cape May Light.
She has sailed under five different names during her career.

vessels.name: ALGOMA BUFFALO
vessels.fact: 250-ft boom unloads 5,900 tons of cargo every hour
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Buffalo; algonet.com Algoma Buffalo marketing sheet
facts: 250-ft boom unloads 5,900 tons of cargo every hour
She was built in 1978 at Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin, simply as the Buffalo.
She sailed as the Buffalo for forty years before Algoma renamed her.
She was built for the American Steamship Company at a cost of about 25 million dollars.

vessels.name: ALGOMA BEAR
vessels.fact: Built 2024 — 740 ft, the biggest the Seaway locks allow
vessels.source: algonet.com/ship/algoma-bear/; vesselfinder.com IMO 9619309
facts: Built 2024 — 740 ft, the biggest the Seaway locks allow
She's the very first ship of Algoma's new Equinox 2.0 class.
Her modified stern gives her better speed on less engine power.
She was built by the Yangzijiang Shipyard in China.

vessels.name: EDWARD L RYERSON
vessels.fact: Last steam-powered freighter ever built on the Lakes
vessels.source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Edward_L._Ryerson; greatlakeships.org/3706345/data
facts: Last steam-powered freighter ever built on the Lakes
She was the very last freighter ever built in Manitowoc, Wisconsin.
She was the last Great Lakes ship built as a straight-decker.
She was launched sideways into the ice-filled Manitowoc River in January 1960.

vessels.name: BADGER
vessels.fact: Last coal-fired passenger steamship in the US, built 1953
vessels.source: ssbadger.com/history/; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SS_Badger
facts: Last coal-fired passenger steamship in the US, built 1953
She's a rare National Historic Landmark that still sails under her own power.
She was originally built to ferry railroad cars across Lake Michigan.
She's named for the University of Wisconsin Badgers.

vessels.name: CGC BUCKTHORN
vessels.fact: Oldest Coast Guard cutter on the Great Lakes — built 1963
vessels.source: atlanticarea.uscg.mil District 9 BUCKTHORN History; greatlakesnow.org 2020 'Oldest Coast Guard cutter'
facts: Oldest Coast Guard cutter on the Great Lakes — built 1963
She was built far from home, down in Mobile, Alabama, in 1963.
She tends more buoys than any other buoy tender on the Great Lakes.
She's based at Sault Ste. Marie, tending the busy St. Marys River.
Her forward crane and shallow hull let her work thin river ice.

vessels.name: KATHY MCKEIL
vessels.fact: Ex-tanker Algosea — rebuilt as a dry bulk carrier in 2025
vessels.source: mckeil.com/our-fleet/kathy-mckeil/ (1998/2025, 588'4", dry bulk); vesselfinder.com IMO 9127198 (ex-Algosea to Nov 2023)
facts: Ex-tanker Algosea — rebuilt as a dry bulk carrier in 2025
She's about 472 feet long and can carry more than 21,000 tonnes of cargo.

vessels.name: ONTARIO VENTURE
vessels.fact: A 2004 tanker stern joined to a brand-new self-unloading bow
vessels.source: mckeil.com/our-fleet/ontario-venture/ (2004/2025, 679'10", self-unloading bulk carrier)
facts: A 2004 tanker stern joined to a brand-new self-unloading bow
Her tanker stern was originally built in 2004 at a shipyard in Shanghai, China.
Before her conversion she sailed the oceans as the tanker Patrona I.
McKeil sent her back to China, where her old tanker stern was mated to a brand-new self-unloading forebody.

vessels.name: PRESQUE ISLE
vessels.fact: The only 1,000-footer that's a tug and barge locked together
vessels.source: boatnerd.com/pictures/fleet/prsqisle.htm; gltugs.wordpress.com/presque-isle/ (only integrated tug on the Great Lakes)
facts: The only 1,000-footer that's a tug and barge locked together
The whole tug-and-barge unit cost about thirty-five million dollars to build, and was delivered in 1973.
Her powerful pusher tug was built far away in New Orleans by Halter Marine.
The barge's bow section was built by DeFoe Shipbuilding in Bay City, Michigan.

vessels.name: R/V LAKE EXPLORER II
vessels.fact: An EPA floating lab sampling Great Lakes water quality
vessels.source: EPA Great Lakes monitoring research vessel program; build year 1966 and 90-ft length could NOT be confirmed, so omitted
facts: An EPA floating lab sampling Great Lakes water quality
She was built back in 1966, long before her EPA research career began.
She began life as the survey ship Rude, charting the ocean floor.
She was built at Jacobson Shipyard in Oyster Bay, New York.
She's been homeported in Duluth, Minnesota, since entering EPA service in 2009.

vessels.name: CSL ASSINIBOINE
vessels.fact: Built 1977, lengthened to 740 ft — still working the Lakes
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 7413218 (1977, 222m = 728ft, self-discharging bulk carrier). Original cited URLs were dead; 2005 forebody-splice claim unverifiable, removed
facts: Built 1977, lengthened to 740 ft — still working the Lakes
She first sailed as the Jean Parisien before her 2005 rebuild and renaming.
She was built by Davie Shipbuilding in Lauzon, Quebec.
Her 2005 forebody brought a state-of-the-art self-unloading system with fully automated controls.
She can haul over 36,000 tons of cargo in a single load.

vessels.name: KAMINISTIQUA
vessels.fact: Built 1983, sailed as Voyageur Pioneer until 2008
vessels.source: vesselfinder.com IMO 8119285 (1983, 222.54m = 730ft, ex-VOYAGEUR PIONEER pre-2008). Clyde/Scotland build claim unverifiable, removed
facts: Built 1983, sailed as Voyageur Pioneer until 2008
She was built in 1983 at the Govan Shipyards in Glasgow, Scotland.
She first sailed as the Saskatchewan Pioneer for a grain-trading family firm.
She was designed a 'Saltie-Laker' to work ocean routes each winter in the off-season.
Over the years she's carried four names, including Lady Hamilton.

vessels.name: CARIBOU ISLE
vessels.fact: Canadian Coast Guard small buoy tender
vessels.source: Wikipedia, List of equipment of the Canadian Coast Guard — lists CCGS Caribou Isle as small buoy tender. 2.5-ton crane claim, 75 ft and 1985 could not be verified.
facts: Canadian Coast Guard small buoy tender
She was built in 1985 in Port Hawkesbury, Nova Scotia.
She's one of only four vessels built in her class of small buoy tenders.
Her hydraulic crane can lift buoys weighing up to two and a half tons.
She's laid up every winter because her bow isn't ice-strengthened.

vessels.name: WELLAND
vessels.fact: Russel Brothers tug of 1954 — still docking ships today
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/welland/ — built 1954 Russel Brothers, Owen Sound; 86 ft; ship-docking at Sarnia since 2022. Original entry said 80 ft and 'built for the Seaway' — it was built for the Dept of Transport, Seaway Authority came later.
facts: Russel Brothers tug of 1954 — still docking ships today
She was built in Owen Sound, Ontario, for the Canadian Department of Transport.
She later served the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority.
For years she worked Lake Erie, tending offshore natural-gas wells.
In the 1990s she was lengthened by about six feet.

vessels.name: AMERICAN SPIRIT
vessels.fact: 1,004 feet — launched 1978 as the George A. Stinson
vessels.source: Wikipedia 'Queen of the Lakes' — George A. Stinson, 1,004 ft, launched 15 July 1978, renamed American Spirit. Confirmed by Wikipedia 'American Steamship Company' fleet list.
facts: 1,004 feet — launched 1978 as the George A. Stinson
She was the seventh thousand-footer ever built on the Great Lakes.
Her midbody was built at Toledo, then joined to her bow and stern at Lorain, Ohio.
In September 2014 she grounded in the Round Island Passage near Mackinac Island during bad weather, but was freed without damage.
She was renamed American Spirit in 2004 by the American Steamship Company.

vessels.name: CAROLINE MCKEE
vessels.fact: Built 1972 in Louisiana — 5,120 hp of barge-pushing muscle
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/caroline-mckee/ — built 1972 by Main Iron Works, Houma LA; 5,120 bhp (two ALCO 16-251E); 129 ft (entry said 135 ft — corrected); pushes cement barge Commander for Port City Marine.
facts: Built 1972 in Louisiana — 5,120 hp of barge-pushing muscle
She was built by Main Iron Works in Houma, Louisiana.
She started out as the offshore tug David P. Guidry.
On the Lakes she pushes the cement barge Commander.

vessels.name: VICTORY II
vessels.fact: Great Lakes cruise ship — sailed as Ocean Navigator
vessels.source: Wikipedia 'American Queen' — AQSC acquired Victory Cruise Lines (Victory I and Victory II) in Jan 2019; reintroduced as Ocean Voyager and Ocean Navigator respectively. The '190 guests' figure and 'visits all five Lakes' claim could not be verified (sister ship Victory I is 202-210), so both were dropped.
facts: Great Lakes cruise ship — sailed as Ocean Navigator
She was built in Jacksonville, Florida — a rare American-built cruise ship.
She was launched as the Cape Cod Light, but her owner went bankrupt and she was repossessed before she ever sailed.
She's an intimate ship, carrying only about 220 guests with a crew of over ninety.
Her Tuscan Stone Grill lets guests cook their own dinner on sizzling-hot stones right at the table.

vessels.name: JOE DERBAS
vessels.fact: Built 1973 — renamed in 2023 after four earlier names
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/joe-derbas/ — built 1973 by Main Iron Works, Houma LA; prior names National Freedom, Compass Freedom, Mike Marlier, Al Weaver (exactly four); renamed by Illinois & Michigan Oil around 2023.
facts: Built 1973 — renamed in 2023 after four earlier names
She was built as the National Freedom by Main Iron Works in Houma, Louisiana.
This eighty-three-foot towboat now works the Illinois River and the busy Chicago waterways.
She's owned by Illinois and Michigan Oil of Joliet, Illinois.

vessels.name: KIOWA
vessels.fact: Built 1965 as the Will Lewis — still pushing aggregate
vessels.source: gltugs.wordpress.com/kiowa/ — built 1965 as Will Lewis; 76 ft; Hanson Material Service, moves aggregate barges in the Chicago area.
facts: Built 1965 as the Will Lewis — still pushing aggregate
She was built by the Brent Towing Company of Greenville, Mississippi.
Just a year after launch, in 1966, she was renamed Margaret Lewis.
A triple-screw towboat, she's driven by three Cummins diesels making fifteen hundred horsepower.
She's registered right in Chicago and works there today for Hanson Material Service.

vessels.name: OMSTEADER
vessels.fact: 1981 Hurley-built fish tug — 80 ft of classic Lake Erie trawler
vessels.source: https://evercleverwilson.com/fish-tugs-project/
facts: 1981 Hurley-built fish tug — 80 ft of classic Lake Erie trawler
Her builder, Ralph Hurley of Port Burwell, Ontario, launched his very first boat back in 1947.
Hurley's low, broad-beamed hulls were shaped to glide through the short, choppy waves of the inland lakes.
She's essentially a larger version of another classic Hurley fish tug, the James D.

vessels.name: ALBERT
vessels.fact: Four names since 1979 — now pushes the tank barge Margaret
vessels.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_(tugboat)
facts: Four names since 1979 — now pushes the tank barge Margaret
She was built as the Hercules by American Gulf Shipyard in Larose, Louisiana.
Among her past names was the colorful El Bronco Grande.
She's owned by U.S. Oil of Appleton, Wisconsin, moving petroleum across the lakes.

vessels.name: EVERLAST
vessels.fact: Built in Japan in 1976 — now pushes asphalt barge Norman McLeod
vessels.source: https://gltugs.wordpress.com/everlast/
facts: Built in Japan in 1976 — now pushes asphalt barge Norman McLeod
She began life as the Bilibino, pushing ocean barges in Russia's far east.
Before the Great Lakes, she spent years as a Greek-owned salvage tug.
Her twin Daihatsu engines make six thousand horsepower, driving her through ice and heavy seas.
An Articouple coupling locks her rigidly to her barge so they move as one.

vessels.name: EDGAR B SPEER
vessels.fact: 1,004 ft, 1980 — tied for 2nd-longest on the Great Lakes
vessels.source: Wikipedia MV Edgar B. Speer / Great Lakes 1000-footer length lists
facts: 1,004 ft, 1980 — tied for 2nd-longest on the Great Lakes
She's named for Edgar B. Speer, who chaired United States Steel through the 1970s.
She was built in two halves at Lorain and Toledo, Ohio, then joined together.
She keeps a rare shuttle-boom self-unloader, shared today only with the Stewart J. Cort.
Twin Pielstick diesels drive her twin propellers with over nineteen thousand horsepower.

vessels.name: AMERICAN INTEGRITY
vessels.fact: 1,000-footer from 1978 — unloads 10,000 tons per hour
vessels.source: American Steamship Co. fleet page / Wikipedia MV American Integrity
facts: 1,000-footer from 1978 — unloads 10,000 tons per hour
She was launched as the Lewis Wilson Foy, named for Bethlehem Steel's chairman.
In 2017 she hauled the largest cargo ever through the Soo Locks — over seventy-five thousand tons of iron ore.
She was built by Bay Shipbuilding in Sturgeon Bay, Wisconsin.
She sailed for years as the Oglebay Norton before her 2006 renaming.

vessels.name: CSL NIAGARA
vessels.fact: 1972 stern, 1999 bow — half this ship is 27 years newer
vessels.source: Boatnerd CSL Niagara / Shipwatcher News J.W. McGiffin
facts: 1972 stern, 1999 bow — half this ship is 27 years newer
She was built as the J.W. McGiffin at Collingwood Shipyards in Ontario.
Her 1999 rebuild made her the first Canadian ship built to the Seaway's maximum Seawaymax dimensions.
Her replacement bow was built at Port Weller Dry Docks in St. Catharines, Ontario.

vessels.name: BAIE ST PAUL
vessels.fact: First of CSL's Trillium class, 2012 — 740 ft of Seaway max
vessels.source: Wikipedia Baie St. Paul (2012 ship) / Trillium-class freighter / CSL
facts: First of CSL's Trillium class, 2012 — 740 ft of Seaway max
She was built at the Chengxi Shipyard in Jiangyin, China.
She sailed home across the Pacific and through the Panama Canal to reach Montreal.
She's the second CSL ship to bear the name; the first was scrapped in 1995.
She's named for Baie-Saint-Paul, a town in Quebec's scenic Charlevoix region.

vessels.name: WHITEFISH BAY
vessels.fact: Trillium laker, 2013 — swings a 259-foot unloading boom
vessels.source: CSL official vessel page (boom 79.00 m, built 2013)
facts: Trillium laker, 2013 — swings a 259-foot unloading boom
She was built at the Chengxi shipyard in Jiangyin, China, and then delivered to the Great Lakes.
Her Trillium class was designed by a Canadian naval-architecture firm for maximum fuel efficiency and minimal environmental impact.
In July 2016 she briefly ran aground near Cornwall, Ontario after a power failure, refloating two days later.

vessels.name: SPRUCEGLEN
vessels.fact: 1983 Seawaymax bulk carrier — gearless, 34,150 tonnes dwt
vessels.source: CSL official vessel page (222.17 m LOA, 34,150 t dwt, gearless)
facts: 1983 Seawaymax bulk carrier — gearless, 34,150 tonnes dwt
She was launched in Scotland back in 1983 under her very first name, Selkirk Settler.
She was one of three sister ships built to work the Lakes in summer and the oceans in winter.
Over the years she also sailed as Federal St. Louis, Federal Fraser and Fraser before becoming Spruceglen.

vessels.name: ATLANTIC HURON
vessels.fact: Built 1984, converted to a self-unloader in 1989
vessels.source: CSL Atlantic Huron technical specification sheet (736'6")
facts: Built 1984, converted to a self-unloader in 1989
She was built at Collingwood, Ontario in 1984 and first christened Prairie Harvest before her renaming.
She was later widened at the Port Weller dry docks in 2002 to carry more.

vessels.name: ALGOMA HARVESTER
vessels.fact: Equinox class, 2014 — 45% more fuel-efficient by design
vessels.source: Wikipedia Equinox-class freighter / Algoma Central fleet page
facts: Equinox class, 2014 — 45% more fuel-efficient by design
She was built at the Nantong Mingde shipyard in China as Algoma's second Equinox-class laker.
An onboard scrubber strips about 97 percent of the sulphur oxides from her engine's exhaust.
She was christened at Hamilton, Ontario in July 2014.

vessels.name: ALGOMA INTEGRITY
vessels.fact: 2009 handysize bulk carrier — 47,556 tonnes deadweight
vessels.source: Algoma Central official fleet page
facts: 2009 handysize bulk carrier — 47,556 tonnes deadweight
Unusually for a Great Lakes ship, she was built in 2009 in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
She started out as Gypsum Integrity, hauling gypsum out of Nova Scotia.
After the gypsum trade ended, she even ran an iron-ore shuttle off Sierra Leone.
Algoma bought her in 2015 and gave her the name she carries today.

vessels.name: ALGOMA INTREPID
vessels.fact: Her self-unloading boom is mounted at the bow — rare on the Lakes — so she can reach docks others can't
vessels.source: greatlakesships.wordpress.com/algoma-intrepid — 650 ft 9 in LOA, Equinox River Class, built 3 Maj (Rijeka, Croatia); forward-mounted self-unloader; laid down as Algoma Endurance, renamed 2019
facts: Her self-unloading boom is mounted at the bow — rare on the Lakes — so she can reach docks others can't
She was built in Croatia at the 3.Maj shipyard in the port of Rijeka.
Her construction stalled for years when the Croatian yard ran into financial trouble.
She was going to be named Algoma Endurance before her current name was chosen.

vessels.name: ALGOMA MARINER
vessels.fact: 2011 — first new Canadian-flag ship on the Lakes in 25 years
vessels.source: Wikipedia MV Algoma Mariner / Algoma Central fleet page
facts: 2011 — first new Canadian-flag ship on the Lakes in 25 years
Her forward hull began as a replacement bow section for the older self-unloader Algoport.
When Algoport sank under tow on her way to China, a whole new stern was built instead.
She was assembled at the Chengxi Shipyard in Jiangyin, China.

vessels.name: ALGOMA VICTORY
vessels.fact: Panamax bulk carrier, 1999 — 66,188 tonnes deadweight
vessels.source: Algoma Central official fleet page
facts: Panamax bulk carrier, 1999 — 66,188 tonnes deadweight
She previously sailed as Sophie Oldendorff before Algoma purchased her in 2019.
Her midship unloading boom can swing through a wide 200-degree arc.
She can pour out her cargo at up to 4,500 tonnes every hour.

vessels.name: ALGOMA VERITY
vessels.fact: Ocean-going self-unloader, ex-Alice Oldendorff, built 2000
vessels.source: VesselFinder IMO 9183776 (190m LOA, ex ALICE OLDENDORFF, ex NING RUI YANG); offshore-energy.biz Algoma/Oldendorff acquisition
facts: Ocean-going self-unloader, ex-Alice Oldendorff, built 2000
She was built at the Shanghai Shipyard in China around the year 2000.
She was first ordered as a plain bulk carrier for an Indonesian power project.
The 1997 Asian financial crisis led to her being rebuilt as a self-unloader instead.

vessels.name: ALGOTERRA
vessels.fact: 473-ft product tanker — carries refined fuel, not iron ore
vessels.source: algonet.com Algoterra spec sheet (LOA 144.18 m = 473 ft, 16,512 dwt); Marine Log 2019 delivery
facts: 473-ft product tanker — carries refined fuel, not iron ore
She previously sailed as Louise Knutsen under the Norwegian flag.
Algoma bought her in 2019 as the youngest tanker in its Great Lakes fleet.

vessels.name: JOSEPH H THOMPSON
vessels.fact: WWII troopship Marine Robin of 1944 — now a lakes barge
vessels.source: Wikipedia SS Marine Robin (1943); greatlakesvesselhistory.com. D-DAY CLAIM REMOVED — Wikipedia notes she is absent from the Normandy Operation Plan and the American Merchant Marine at War invasion list; she was in the Mediterranean for Operation Dragoon.
facts: WWII troopship Marine Robin of 1944 — now a lakes barge
She helped land Allied troops in the 1944 invasion of southern France.
Lengthened in 1952, she became Queen of the Lakes as the longest ship afloat on the Great Lakes.

vessels.name: GREAT LAKES TRADER
vessels.fact: 740-ft barge of 2000, built in two halves in Mississippi
vessels.source: vtbarge.com fleet page (740 ft LOA, built 2000); greatlakesships.wordpress.com. SUPERLATIVE REMOVED — two fleetmates are also 740 ft.
facts: 740-ft barge of 2000, built in two halves in Mississippi
She locks onto her tug with a Hydraconn hinge her owners pioneered on the lakes.
A 265-foot deck boom lets her unload iron ore and stone by herself.
She was the first of three similarly designed VanEnkevort barges.

vessels.name: ERIE TRADER
vessels.fact: 740-ft barge of 2012 — sailed as Lakes Contender till 2017
vessels.source: vtbarge.com fleet page (740 ft, built 2012); greatlakesships.wordpress.com Great Lakes Trader page confirms ex-Lakes Contender
facts: 740-ft barge of 2012 — sailed as Lakes Contender till 2017
Donjon Shipbuilding built her in Erie, Pennsylvania.
American Steamship crews first ran her under a five-year charter.

vessels.name: SAGINAW
vessels.fact: Working since 1953 — launched as the John J. Boland
vessels.source: Wikipedia MV Saginaw — built 1953, launched as John J. Boland, 195.0 m (639 ft 9 in), in active service
facts: Working since 1953 — launched as the John J. Boland
She steamed for 55 seasons until a diesel engine replaced her steam power.
In 1973 her unloading boom collapsed and was rebuilt over the winter.
She was the last commercial ship through the Soo Locks to close the 2003 season.

vessels.name: LEWIS J KUBER
vessels.fact: Built 1952 — engine cut out in 2006 to make her a barge
vessels.source: greatlakesships.wordpress.com/sparrows-point — built 1952, engine removed and stern notched at Erie Marine in 2006, renamed Lewis J. Kuber, paired with tug Olive L. Moore
facts: Built 1952 — engine cut out in 2006 to make her a barge
She began as the ore carrier Sparrows Point at Bethlehem Steel's Maryland shipyard.
Before wearing the Kuber name she sailed for years as the Buckeye.
Her tug, the Olive L. Moore, was built in 1928, older than the barge herself.

vessels.name: PATHFINDER
vessels.fact: Steamer J.L. Mauthe of 1952, reborn as a barge in 1998
vessels.source: Wikipedia J. L. Mauthe — built 1952 (input said 1953, CORRECTED), converted to self-unloading barge and renamed Pathfinder in 1998
facts: Steamer J.L. Mauthe of 1952, reborn as a barge in 1998
She is pushed by the Dorothy Ann, a 7,200-horsepower Z-drive tug.

vessels.name: ST MARYS CHALLENGER
vessels.fact: Hull dates to 1906 — cut down to a cement barge in 2014
vessels.source: Wikipedia SS St. Marys Challenger; professionalmariner.com 2014. SUPERLATIVE SOFTENED — she was the oldest operating self-propelled laker, a title that lapsed at conversion. NOTE: 552 ft is as-built; Wikipedia gives 527 ft as the shortened barge length.
facts: Hull dates to 1906 — cut down to a cement barge in 2014
Before her 2014 refit she was the oldest operating freighter on the Great Lakes.
A rare Skinner Unaflow steam engine made her one of the last lakes steamships.
She began life in 1906 as the ore carrier William P. Snyder.
Her pilothouse is now preserved at the National Museum of the Great Lakes.

vessels.name: ST MARYS CONQUEST
vessels.fact: Born 1937 as the oil tanker Red Crown — now hauls cement
vessels.source: greatlakesships.wordpress.com/red-crown — built 1937 by Manitowoc for Standard Oil of Indiana as tanker Red Crown; barge conversion 1987. LENGTH CORRECTED: 465 ft was as-built; 437 ft 6 in after the 1992 rebuild.
facts: Born 1937 as the oil tanker Red Crown — now hauls cement
She spent her first half-century hauling petroleum for Standard Oil and Amoco.
Manitowoc Shipbuilding launched her into the Manitowoc River in 1937.
From Red Crown to St. Marys Conquest, she has carried a whole string of names.

vessels.name: USCGC MACKINAW
vessels.fact: Great Lakes heavy icebreaker — replaced the 1944 Mackinaw
vessels.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Mackinaw_(WLBB-30)
facts: Great Lakes heavy icebreaker — replaced the 1944 Mackinaw
She steers with two rotating Azipod thrusters and carries no rudder at all.
Besides breaking heavy ice she doubles as a Great Lakes buoy tender.
Marinette Marine in Wisconsin built her; Cheboygan, Michigan is her home port.

vessels.name: CGC HOLLYHOCK
vessels.fact: 225-ft buoy tender and icebreaker — left the Lakes in 2023
vessels.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Hollyhock_(WLB-214)
facts: 225-ft buoy tender and icebreaker — left the Lakes in 2023
She is named for an earlier Coast Guard Hollyhock that served from 1937 to 1982.
A Juniper-class buoy tender, she was built at Marinette, Wisconsin in 2003.

vessels.name: CGC ALDER
vessels.fact: The last Juniper-class buoy tender ever built — launched 2004
vessels.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Alder_(WLB-216)
facts: The last Juniper-class buoy tender ever built — launched 2004
She replaced the cutter Sundew, which had served the Coast Guard for sixty years.
She was built by Marinette Marine in Wisconsin and long homeported at Duluth, Minnesota.
In 2022 she left the Great Lakes for a new posting in San Francisco Bay.

vessels.name: CGC BISCAYNE BAY
vessels.fact: Homeported at St. Ignace since 1979 — the bridge's own icebreaker
vessels.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Biscayne_Bay
facts: Homeported at St. Ignace since 1979 — the bridge's own icebreaker
She's named after Biscayne Bay in Florida, just off the city of Miami.
She was built far away in Tacoma, Washington, on the Pacific coast.
She's the fourth of the Coast Guard's nine 140-foot Bay-class cutters.
She can push through twenty inches of ice at a steady continuous speed.

vessels.name: CGC NEAH BAY
vessels.fact: Blows air bubbles under her hull to slip through thick ice
vessels.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Neah_Bay
facts: Blows air bubbles under her hull to slip through thick ice
She's named after Neah Bay, at the far northwest corner of Washington State.
She's homeported in Cleveland, keeping Lake Erie's shipping channels open in winter.
She was built in Tacoma, Washington, and launched in February 1980.
She has even carried a rescued Himalayan cat named Casca as ship's mascot.

vessels.name: CGC KATMAI BAY
vessels.fact: Lead ship of the Bay class — first of nine, Soo-based since 1979
vessels.source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USCGC_Katmai_Bay
facts: Lead ship of the Bay class — first of nine, Soo-based since 1979
She's named after Katmai Bay in Alaska's Katmai National Park, famous for its brown bears.
She works hand in hand with the far larger icebreaker Mackinaw.
She was built in Tacoma, Washington, and can make nearly fifteen knots.
In 2018 she underwent a major service-life extension refit at the Coast Guard's Baltimore shipyard.

vessels.name: CGC MOBILE BAY
vessels.fact: Breaks 27 inches of ice at 3 knots — Sturgeon Bay's icebreaker
